title: How Haunted House Attractions Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and business of haunted house attractions, from ancient Egyptian grave traps and Greek/Roman mazes, through medieval scare plays, Shakespeare, Victorian spiritualism and wax museums, Pepper's ghost, and early dark rides, to the Disneyland Haunted Mansion, the Jaycees' fundraising haunted houses of the 1970s-80s, and the commercial haunts of the 1990s onward. They cover running a haunted house (per-square-foot costs, theme changes, throughput, scaring forward, scare pockets, compressed-air effects), the 1984 fire at Six Flags Great Adventure's haunted house, extreme haunts like McCamy Manner, and church-run hell houses. The episode closes with horror movie chat, a BuzzFeed photo list, and listener mail about The Karate Kid.
topics: Six Flags Great Adventure haunted house fire

entities.name: Stuff You Missed in History Class

segments.title: Opening banter and haunted house statistics
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Halloween-week episode, note haunted attractions are everywhere (professional, theme park, and charity), and cite National Retail Federation figures on attendance and Halloween spending. They also briefly discuss decorating for Halloween.

segments.title: Ancient and classical origins of scares
segments.summary: The hosts trace early scare attractions to ancient Egypt, where traps and creepy devices protected graves, and to Greek and Roman mazes with monsters and early stage effects like fake blood. They connect these to the theater tradition.

segments.title: Medieval plays, Shakespeare, Victorian era and wax museums
segments.summary: Medieval scare plays used gore to encourage piety, Shakespeare used ghosts and monsters, and Victorian spiritualism and wax museums with horror tableaux laid groundwork for haunted houses. Pepper's ghost illusion is introduced.

segments.title: Dark rides and early haunted attractions
segments.summary: Twentieth-century dark rides, traveling freak shows, and abandoned old houses are cited as progenitors. The hosts describe the first recorded haunted attraction at the 1915 Edwardian Fair and the Grand Guignol-style French precedent, then the Haunted Mansion at Disneyland (1969), which began as a walkthrough and became a dark ride, and was based on the Winchester Mystery House.

segments.title: Jaycees and the rise of commercial haunted houses
segments.summary: The United States Junior Chamber (Jaycees) popularized community haunted-house fundraisers in the 1970s. Bloomington, Illinois members Jim Goulden and Tom Hillegas created a how-to package through the Haunted House Company. Private companies followed in the 1990s, with Another World in Atlanta and Thirteen Story in New Orleans cited. Church haunted houses are mentioned.

segments.title: Horror movie recommendations and themed haunts
segments.summary: Hosts swap horror movie picks, including The Woman in Black, The Innkeepers, and The House of the Devil, and discuss Rob Zombie's Great American Nightmare haunt, which drew criticism for a John Wayne Gacy room. Themes and the American Horror Story clown are mentioned.

segments.title: Running a haunted house: costs, safety, and the Six Flags fire
segments.summary: Costs run about fifteen dollars per square foot for decorations and effects. Operators must change themes and layouts yearly and balance business sense with safety. The 1984 fire at Six Flags Great Adventure's modular haunted dark ride killed eight teenagers and led to sprinkler and exit-sign changes. A Creepy World employee was caught in a noose and survived with brain damage.

segments.title: Throughput, scaring forward, scare pockets, and special effects
segments.summary: The hosts explain throughput, the timing of groups (about one group every thirty seconds), scaring forward so groups do not collide, scare pockets with hidden actors who scramble back, and compressed-air effects triggered by motion sensors or touch pads that randomize scares.

segments.title: Extreme haunted houses and McCamy Manner
segments.summary: Extreme haunts that involve physical contact are discussed, including McCamy Manner in San Diego, which takes four people a day, requires an application and a waiver, and is said to have no safe word. Similar extreme haunts are named in New York, Los Angeles, and Las Vegas. Hosts criticize extreme haunts for lacking story buildup, contrasting them with slasher and psychological thrillers like Wolf Creek.

segments.title: Hell houses
segments.summary: Church-run hell houses, which scare visitors into religious conversion, are described. Jerry Falwell is credited with starting them in the 1970s, and the Abundant Life Christian Center in Cedar Hill, Texas, later packaged them with purchasable modules such as an abortion room, AIDS room, and lesbian suicide room, ending in a depiction of Hell and an altar call. The documentary Hell House and a Vice article are referenced.

segments.title: Scared face photos and wrap-up
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a BuzzFeed list of scared-face photos from haunted houses. Josh closes the topic and invites listeners to search for more information.

segments.title: Listener mail: The Karate Kid
segments.summary: A listener writes about the Karate Kid episode, describing nostalgia and sharing that they sent the film to a six-year-old nephew. Josh mentions a cover of The Best Around by The Bangalores.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts list ways to contact the show and sign off.
